claims.text: Adjusting elemental proportions in a lightweight high-entropy alloy will improve its mechanical performance relative to an unmodified baseline.
Adjusting elemental proportions in a lightweight high-entropy alloy will improve its corrosion resistance relative to an unmodified baseline.
Adjusting elemental proportions in a lightweight high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to an unmodified baseline.
The compositionally modified alloy will retain low density.
The intervention is to adjust the proportions of elements in the alloy.
Changing elemental proportions will produce microstructural refinement.
A sluggish-diffusion effect will contribute to the predicted property improvements.
Formation of protective oxides will contribute to improved corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The hypothesis is intended to hold under high-temperature conditions.
There are upper-temperature limits beyond which the expected benefits may not hold.
High-temperature exposure may alter alloy microstructure and properties.
Elemental proportions can be varied systematically and the resulting mechanical, corrosion, oxidation, and microstructural responses measured.
Failure of composition adjustment to improve mechanical performance, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
